```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(checktor)
```


## Close the gap

`R CMD check` tells you whether your package builds, installs and runs. CRAN
volunteers also read each new package by hand, and they ask for more. They
object to a help page with no `\value{}`, a `set.seed()` buried inside a
function and a Description one line long. `R CMD check` passes all three
without a word, and any one of them can send a package back.

![Seven package problems in a grid against `R CMD check`, lintr and checktor, with a filled dot where each one catches the problem. `R CMD check` alone catches undocumented arguments, and lintr alone catches a line over 80 characters. lintr and checktor both catch a bare `T` in place of `TRUE`, and `R CMD check` and checktor both catch a Title not in title case. Only checktor catches the last three, a `set.seed()` left in a function, a one-line Description and a missing `\value{}` tag.](figures/coverage-light.svg){.ct-fig .ct-light}
![](figures/coverage-dark.svg){.ct-fig .ct-dark aria-hidden="true"}

checktor holds your package to the rules reviewers apply by hand. They come
from the [CRAN Repository
Policy](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/policies.html), [Writing R
Extensions](https://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/r-release/R-exts.html) and
the [CRAN Cookbook](https://contributor.r-project.org/cran-cookbook/), the R
Contributor guide to the problems that get packages sent back. Use it alongside
`R CMD check`, which remains the authority on whether a package builds and runs,
and [lintr](https://lintr.r-lib.org), which is the place for code style.

## Install checktor

Install the release from CRAN.

```{r eval=FALSE}
install.packages("checktor")
```

The development version carries changes that have not reached CRAN yet. Install
it from GitHub.

```{r eval=FALSE}
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("coatless-rpkg/checktor")
```

## Run a first checkup

Load the package.

```{r}
library(checktor)
```

`checktor()` examines a package directory. Rather than experiment on your own
package, start with a throwaway one. `example_diagnose_scenario()` builds a small
package around one file of bad habits and returns its path.

```{r}
pkg <- example_diagnose_scenario("code_examples/tf_usage_bad.R",
                                 show_content = FALSE)
```

The file uses `T` and `F` where it means `TRUE` and `FALSE`.

```{r}
#| label: show-bad-file
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
src <- readLines(file.path(pkg, "R", "tf_usage_bad.R"))
cat("```r\n", paste(src, collapse = "\n"), "\n```\n", sep = "")
```

> `example_diagnose_scenario()` prints the file itself unless you pass
> `show_content = FALSE`. This page passes `FALSE` and shows the file above as
> highlighted R instead of console output.

Now the checkup itself.

```{r}
# verbose and progress are off here, which keeps the printout compact
results <- checktor(pkg, verbose = FALSE, progress = FALSE)
results
```

The printout marks each of the five categories (code, DESCRIPTION,
documentation, general and CRAN policy) as healthy or failing. It lists any
check that did not run and ends with the package's overall health. Here the code
category fails on seven uses of `T` and `F`. `url_liveness` did not run, because
it fetches URLs only when you are at the console.

Each check has one of three severities. `policy` marks a rule CRAN applies,
`robustness` a defect CRAN would still accept, and `opinion` a convention. By
default, overall health counts policy and robustness findings and leaves opinion
findings out of the count.

![Three severities side by side. Policy breaks a CRAN rule, such as `set.seed(42)` inside a function. Robustness is a real defect that CRAN still accepts, such as `sorted = F`. Opinion is a convention with no rule behind it, such as a help page with no `\value{}`. Under policy and robustness, a bracket reads Counts toward overall health. Under opinion, a dashed bracket reads Listed, not counted.](figures/severity-light.svg){.ct-fig .ct-light}
![](figures/severity-dark.svg){.ct-fig .ct-dark aria-hidden="true"}

[Where the Checks Come From](check-sources.html) gives the source and severity
of every check, and the [function
reference](https://r-pkg.thecoatlessprofessor.com/checktor/reference/index.html)
documents each one.

> On your own package, call `checktor()` with no arguments. It finds the package
> root from anywhere inside it, so a working directory of `R/` or
> `tests/testthat/` still examines the whole package.

## Read the results as data

The printed report is for people. To filter, count or reshape the findings, use
the accessors, which return plain data frames.

![One `checktor_results` object feeds three plain data frames. `summary()` gives one row per category, counting the checks that passed, failed and were skipped. `issues()` gives one row per issue, with its severity, file and line. `tidy()` gives one row per check, with its severity and whether it passed or was skipped.](figures/result-shapes-light.svg){.ct-fig .ct-light}
![](figures/result-shapes-dark.svg){.ct-fig .ct-dark aria-hidden="true"}

```{r}
summary(results)   # one row per category
```

```{r}
issues(results)    # one row per issue, with file and line
```

`tidy(results)` gives one row per check, passed or not, and `as.data.frame()`
returns the same frame. Its `skipped` column marks a check that did not run, such
as the URL fetch above, so a check that sat out never reads as a pass.
`summary()` counts that check as skipped, and its `passed`, `failed` and
`skipped` columns add up to `checks`.

Three helpers answer the usual questions.

```{r}
is_healthy(results)
n_issues(results)
failed_checks(results)
```

`is_healthy()` and `n_issues()` follow the overall health, so by default they
count only policy and robustness findings. `issues()` lists findings of every
severity, opinion included, and `failed_checks()` lists every check that failed.
Every accessor also works on a single category, as in
`issues(results$code_issues)`. `issues()`, `n_issues()`, `is_healthy()` and
`passed()` work on a single check as well.

## Gate a script on one call

`checkup()` runs the same diagnosis without printing and returns one logical,
`TRUE` when the package is in good overall health.

```{r}
checkup(pkg)
```

It is built to end a shell one-liner. [checktor in Continuous
Integration](checktor-in-ci.html) puts it in charge of a GitHub Actions build.

## Treat what it finds

Diagnosis without treatment is only bad news. `prescribe()` takes each failed
check in turn and prints its findings, its remedy and a before-and-after example.

```{r}
prescribe(results)
```

`health_report()` writes the same findings and remedies to a file, as Markdown,
HTML or plain text, to keep beside your `cran-comments.md`.

```{r eval=FALSE}
health_report(results, file = "package-health.md")
health_report(results, file = "package-health.html", format = "html")
```

## Examine one category at a time

Each category also runs on its own. That helps when you are fixing one thing and
would rather not hear about the rest.

```{r eval=FALSE}
diagnose_code_issues()           # just the R sources
diagnose_description_issues()    # just DESCRIPTION
diagnose_documentation_issues()  # help pages, examples, vignettes, demos
diagnose_general_issues()        # size, URLs, NEWS, README links
diagnose_policy_violations()     # CRAN policy
```

To run one check, call its `lab_*()` function, such as `lab_tf_usage()`.

## Check only what CRAN receives

`R CMD build` leaves out whatever `.Rbuildignore` matches, and checktor leaves
out the same files. Help pages and vignettes that never reach the tarball are
never checked.

The [devtag](https://github.com/moodymudskipper/devtag) package uses this to
document unexported functions. Its `@dev` tag writes the help page and adds the
`.Rd` file to `.Rbuildignore`, so contributors see the page and users do not.
Examples on those pages can call `:::` without an objection from checktor. The
pkgdown-only articles that `usethis::use_article()` writes to
`vignettes/articles/` are left out the same way.

`roxygen_usage` is the exception. It reads all of `man/`, because it asks
whether your working tree matches roxygen, which is a question about your files
rather than the tarball.

## Turn down the volume

`checktor()` is chatty by design. In a script, quiet it once and every later
call inherits the setting.

```{r eval=FALSE}
configure_doctor(verbose_default = FALSE, progress_default = FALSE)

# or per call
results <- checktor(verbose = FALSE, progress = FALSE)
```

## Ask for a check, or turn one off

Some checks never join a run. Either no authority backs them, or they concern
your submission workflow rather than the package. Nothing tried to run them, so
they are not reported as skipped, and a quiet run does not mention them. The
results list them.

```{r}
results$metadata$on_request_checks
```

Each is a `lab_*()` function like any other check, so running one takes one
call.

```{r}
lab_cran_comments_file(pkg, verbose = FALSE)
```

In the other direction, you can turn off a check you have decided against. For
one package, list it in that package's `DESCRIPTION`.

```yaml
Config/checktor/disable: news_file
```

The same `DESCRIPTION` can mute a finding you have reviewed with
`Config/checktor/allow`, and add words to a check's list with fields such as
`Config/checktor/software_names`. These settings travel with the package, so
they apply wherever it is checked.

![The `DESCRIPTION` of mypkg with three `Config/checktor` lines highlighted, under the note Applies wherever the package is checked. `disable: news_file` leaves a check out, so `news_file` never runs. `allow: license_file_unneeded` mutes a reviewed finding, and the run reports it as muted. `software_names: DuckDB` adds a software name, so DuckDB should be in single quotes.](figures/config-fields-light.svg){.ct-fig .ct-light}
![](figures/config-fields-dark.svg){.ct-fig .ct-dark aria-hidden="true"}

For every package, set the option once, for example in `.Rprofile`.

```{r eval=FALSE}
options(checktor.disable = "news_file")
```

Disabled checks do not run and are not counted anywhere. That sets them apart
from skipped checks, which were meant to run and could not.

## Fit it into your workflow

Run checktor between writing code and running `R CMD check`.

```{r eval=FALSE}
devtools::document()
devtools::test()

results <- checktor()  # the extra-CRAN checkup
prescribe(results)     # read the remedies

devtools::check()      # the standard checks
```

`devtools::check()` runs `R CMD check` through the rcmdcheck package, which
also returns the NOTEs, WARNINGs and ERRORs as data you can inspect. checktor's
checkup covers only the rules it knows, so whether the package is worth
submitting remains your call.
